item.title: Can a Wearable Pulse Signal Spot Atrial Fibrillation? Classical Features vs. a 1D CNN
item.dc:creator: Shubham Sendre
item.description:
What This Is (and Isn’t)

Smartwatches detect atrial fibrillation (AFib) from PPG — the optical pulse waveform measured at the wrist or fingertip — not from ECG. This post compares two ways to do that on the same data: a classical pipeline (detect pulses, measure how irregular the intervals are, fit logistic regression) and a small 1D convolutional network on the raw waveform.

It is not a clinical validation. It is 35 patients, bedside-monitor PPG from ICU patients, and a modest sample. The point is how the two approaches behave when the evaluation is done honestly.

The Data

MIMIC PERform AF (Zenodo 6807403, ODbL) is a derived subset of MIMIC-III: 19 AF and 16 non-AF subjects, 20 minutes each, PPG sampled at 125 Hz. It needs no PhysioNet credentialing. Each recording is cut into non-overlapping 30-second windows, giving 1,398 windows (54% AF) after dropping flat or unusable segments.

Method 1: Pulse-Interval Irregularity (NeuroKit2)

AFib is “irregularly irregular”, so the signal of interest is variability in the beat-to-beat interval. For each window:

  1. nk.ppg_process cleans the PPG and detects pulse peaks.
  2. Inter-beat intervals (IBIs) are kept if they imply 30–200 bpm.
  3. Seven features are computed: RMSSD, SDNN, pNN50, coefficient of variation, Poincaré SD1/SD2, turning-point ratio, mean heart rate.
  4. A class-balanced logistic regression is fit on standardized features.

As a floor, a single-feature detector (RMSSD, min-max scaled) is also scored.

Method 2: 1D CNN on the Raw Waveform

Three conv blocks (16/32/64 channels, kernel 7, BatchNorm, ReLU, max-pool 4), global average pooling, dropout 0.3, one logit. Each window is z-scored. 12 epochs of Adam, no augmentation, no tuning.

Evaluation: Subject-Independent or Not at All

Windows from one person are highly correlated, so a random window split lets a model recognise people instead of rhythm and inflates every number. All results here use 5-fold StratifiedGroupKFold grouped by subject: no patient appears in both train and test. Subject-level results average a subject’s window probabilities and threshold at 0.5.

Results

Everything above was repeated over 20 random seeds (each reshuffles which subjects land in which fold, and re-initialises the CNN). Intervals are 95% subject-level bootstrap intervals (2,000 resamples of the 35 patients, scores averaged over the 20 seeds), so they reflect both having only 35 patients and seed-to-seed variation. Windows are resampled with their patient, never separately.

Method (window level) AUROC [95% CI] Sensitivity [95% CI] Specificity [95% CI]
RMSSD only 0.859 [0.697, 0.973] 0.256 [0.155, 0.372] 0.880 [0.718, 0.992]
Classical (7 features + LR) 0.965 [0.908, 0.997] 0.948 [0.912, 0.979] 0.886 [0.742, 0.987]
1D CNN 0.573 [0.433, 0.703] 0.748 [0.652, 0.833] 0.384 [0.236, 0.533]
Method (subject level, n=35) AUROC [95% CI] Sensitivity [95% CI] Specificity [95% CI]
RMSSD only 0.882 [0.705, 1.000] 0.257 [0.095, 0.450] 0.876 [0.688, 1.000]
Classical + LR 0.978 [0.930, 1.000] 1.000 [1.000, 1.000] 0.892 [0.722, 1.000]
1D CNN 0.567 [0.417, 0.708] 0.765 [0.665, 0.856] 0.375 [0.219, 0.536]

What the repeats add:

  • The ranking holds. The classical AUROC interval ([0.91, 1.00]) is far from the CNN’s ([0.43, 0.70]).
  • The CNN is consistent with chance. Its AUROC interval includes 0.5. It is also the unstable one: seed-to-seed SD of AUROC is 0.065, versus 0.018 for the classical model.
  • Sensitivity/specificity for the CNN depend on the seed. My first single-seed run happened to give 0.45 / 0.59; averaged over seeds it is 0.75 / 0.38. The CNN is not reliably leaning either way at a 0.5 threshold, which is itself a sign it learned little.
  • The subject-level sensitivity “1.000 [1.000, 1.000]” is not a guarantee. Every AF patient was flagged in the resamples that contained one, but a bootstrap of 19 patients cannot see a failure that did not occur in the data. The specificity interval ([0.72, 1.00]) is the more honest picture.

Try It: Live Waveform Explorer

The panel below is a marimo notebook running in your browser via WebAssembly. Pick a subject, scrub through three sampled 30-second windows, and see the PPG with detected pulses and the beat-to-beat interval trace (reveal the true label when you’ve guessed). Then drag the threshold slider to see how the classical detector, the CNN, and RMSSD alone trade sensitivity against specificity.

neurokit2, wfdb, and torch aren’t WASM-safe, so pulse detection and model scores were precomputed offline (105 windows, 2 MB). What is live: the interval features for the window you pick and the threshold sweep.

Why the CNN Loses Here

  • Tiny data. ~28 training subjects per fold. A CNN has to discover “interval irregularity” from raw samples; the classical pipeline is handed it by construction.
  • The signal is about timing between beats, not waveform shape. A global pooled CNN with local kernels has no direct route to inter-beat intervals.
  • Untuned. 12 epochs, no augmentation, no early stopping. A tuned or pretrained model could do better — this is a baseline, not a ceiling.

Note also that RMSSD alone has an AUROC of 0.86 but sensitivity of 0.26 at the default threshold: the ranking is good, the operating point is not. Threshold choice matters as much as the model.

Caveats

  • 35 subjects; even the bootstrap intervals above assume these patients are a fair sample of AF/non-AF ICU patients.
  • ICU bedside PPG is cleaner than wrist PPG during daily motion.
  • Non-AF subjects aren’t necessarily healthy; they may have other arrhythmias or ectopy, which the dataset does not break out.
  • The seed-0 run drives the notebook’s waveform scores and ROC curves; the tables above are the 20-seed summary.

Reproducing

make_waveforms.py exports the notebook’s waveform file; notebook.py is the marimo source. generate_artifacts.py (expects the WFDB zips from Zenodo unpacked into data/raw_af/ and data/raw_nonaf/) writes public/artifacts/windows.csv and results.json. Dependencies: neurokit2, wfdb, scikit-learn, torch, pandas.

item.title: Pixi vs. Conda for Production Bioinformatics Environments: Why uv Doesn’t Even Get to Compete
item.dc:creator: Shubham Sendre
item.description:
What This Was Supposed to Be (and Why It Changed)

This started as a straight Pixi-vs-uv comparison: install the same production bioinformatics environment with both, time it, compare lockfiles. That post doesn’t exist, because the premise doesn’t survive contact with reality.

uv cannot install bioconda packages. It is a PyPI-and-Python-interpreter tool, full stop. Its maintainers have an open issue requesting conda-channel support, opened in February 2024, explicitly tagged “not on the immediate roadmap.” STAR, Salmon, samtools, FastQC — the actual tools a pipeline like nf-core/rnaseq depends on — are compiled binaries distributed through bioconda, not Python wheels on PyPI. uv cannot see them, let alone install them.

So this is a Pixi vs. conda/mamba post instead, which is where the real comparison lives. uv gets one section near the end, because Pixi actually uses it internally for the pure-Python slice of a project — that’s the honest role it plays here.

The Task: Reproduce a Real Pipeline’s Dependencies

nf-core/rnaseq is a widely-used, production Nextflow pipeline. I pulled its dependency declarations at tag 3.27.0 — 74 module-level environment.yml files, covering everything from fastqc to bioconductor-deseq2.

The obvious first move — combine all 74 files into one environment and install it once — fails, and how it fails is itself informative.

Finding 1: You Can’t Combine Them Into One Environment

Different modules pin different versions of the same package, because each module only ever runs in its own container or environment in production — nobody has ever needed all 74 to agree on one shared set. Combining them surfaces that immediately:

Package Conflicting pins across modules
python 3.9.18, 3.12.2, 3.12.12, 3.14.5
samtools / htslib 1.21 and 1.24
r-base 4.3 and 4.4.2
gawk 5.1.0 and 5.3.1
sed 4.7 and 4.8

Taking the highest pin for each and resolving the combined set still fails — not just on these six, but broadly. Conda’s solver rejects it on perl=5.26.2 (a 2017 release incompatible with newer package builds), multiqc, preseq, sentieon, and umi_tools, on top of the version splits above. Splitting into three coarser groups (core bioconda tools, the R/Bioconductor stack, sortmerna alone — isolated because its package has Python-build variants that clash with the rest) still doesn’t fully resolve it.

The only granularity that actually works is nf-core’s own: one environment per module. That’s not a limitation of this benchmark — it’s confirmation that nf-core’s container-first design (Docker/Singularity per process, with -profile conda kept as an explicit last resort in its own docs) is the only architecture that was ever going to hold together.

Finding 2: Per-Module, All Three Tools Just Work

With that constraint accepted, I benchmarked conda, mamba, and Pixi installing each of the 74 module environments independently — cold cache (cleared before each tool’s run) and warm cache (repeated right after), one pass each.

Results

Tool Cold total (74 modules) Cold avg/module Warm total Warm avg/module
conda 820.2 s 11.08 s 488.8 s 6.61 s
mamba 683.6 s 9.24 s 381.4 s 5.15 s
Pixi 590.1 s 7.97 s 263.0 s 3.55 s

Pixi wins on both cold and warm installs, and the gap widens on warm cache — 3.55s/module average against conda’s 6.61s, nearly 2x. mamba sits in between, as expected for a faster conda-compatible solver that still shares conda’s package-handling machinery.

An Honest Caveat on These Numbers

This is n=1 per cell — one cold run, one warm run, per tool, per module. These are point estimates, not statistically robust averages. I’d want 3-5 repetitions per cell before trusting the Pixi-vs-mamba gap specifically (9% faster cold, 31% faster warm) to hold up; the conda-vs-Pixi gap is large enough (27% cold, 46% warm) that it’s unlikely to be noise, but treat the exact numbers as directional, not definitive.

One run also hit a real anomaly worth disclosing rather than hiding: Pixi’s cold run on rseqc/junctionannotation initially logged 47,950 seconds — clearly not a real solve time. A clean re-run of the identical spec took 66.5 seconds, in line with six other modules sharing the same two-package set. The likely cause: this machine’s disk hit 99% full partway through the run (my own accumulated package caches were part of that), and I/O under near-zero free space can stall arbitrarily. I’ve reported the clean reproduction value in the table above, not the stall, and disclosed it here instead of pretending it didn’t happen. Five other cells (one mamba failure, four pixi warm-pass failures) failed with explicit ENOSPC errors during that same disk-pressure window and were re-run cleanly afterward with headroom restored.

Finding 3: Reproducibility — Both Work, for Different Reasons

I installed the most complex module (deseq2_qc, 9 packages spanning R and Bioconductor) twice, independently, with both tools, and diffed the result:

  • Pixi: pixi.lock was byte-identical across both installs.
  • conda: conda list --explicit output (which pins exact build strings, not just versions) was also identical across both installs.

Both reproduce exactly here — which isn’t actually the interesting finding, given every package in this test was already pinned to an exact version. The real difference is structural, not about single-run determinism:

  • Pixi generates pixi.lock automatically, every time, covering the whole resolved graph with hashes, committed alongside the project by default.
  • conda’s reproducibility is opt-in and manual. conda create and conda env create -f environment.yml don’t produce a lock file. You have to remember to run conda list --explicit yourself, after the fact, and keep that output somewhere. nf-core’s own module environment.yml files — the actual input to the -profile conda path — carry no lock file at all; they pin top-level versions but say nothing about transitive dependencies or build strings, which can drift as the channel index changes over time.

So the honest claim isn’t “Pixi is more reproducible than conda in a single run” — it’s “Pixi makes reproducibility the default behavior; conda makes it something you have to deliberately opt into and maintain yourself.”

Where uv Actually Fits

uv isn’t absent from this story — it’s just not competing in it. Pixi uses uv internally to resolve and install any PyPI-only dependencies a project declares alongside its conda packages (via Pixi’s [pypi-dependencies] table). So the realistic role for uv in a bioinformatics pipeline isn’t “replace conda” — it’s “handle the pure-Python tooling around the pipeline” — custom analysis scripts, nf-core-tools itself, anything with no bioconda-only binary dependency — while Pixi (or conda/mamba) handles the actual tool binaries. Poetry sits in the same category as uv here: PyPI-only, no bioconda reach, useful for the Python-only slice and nothing else.

Reproducing This

# Pull the pinned pipeline version and extract per-module specs
git clone --depth 1 --branch 3.27.0 https://github.com/nf-core/rnaseq.git

# For a single module, install with each tool (example: fastqc)
conda create -y -p /tmp/env-conda -c conda-forge -c bioconda --override-channels fastqc=0.12.1
mamba create -y -p /tmp/env-mamba -c conda-forge -c bioconda --override-channels fastqc=0.12.1
pixi init /tmp/env-pixi && cd /tmp/env-pixi && pixi add -c conda-forge -c bioconda fastqc==0.12.1

# Reproducibility check
conda list -p /tmp/env-conda --explicit   # re-run install, diff this output
cat pixi.lock                              # re-run pixi install, diff this file

The full per-module benchmark script, the 74-module spec extraction, and the raw results (module_benchmark.csv) are in this post’s source directory.

Questions about the benchmark or the methodology? Connect on LinkedIn.

item.title: AI Bioprivacy: Two Different Problems Hiding Behind One Word
item.dc:creator: Shubham Sendre
item.description:
One Word, Two Problems

“Bioprivacy” sounds like it should mean one thing: keeping biological data private. In practice, the term is doing double duty for two problems that share a prefix and not much else.

Problem one is the one most people mean by default: your genome, your clinical records, your multi-omic data — kept out of the wrong hands, used only with consent, not re-identifiable after the fact. This is Lifebit’s territory — federated analytics platforms that let researchers query biomedical data without ever moving it off the institution that holds it.

Problem two is newer and much stranger: AI is making it easier for anyone to design a dangerous biological agent, and the “privacy” question flips — it’s not about protecting an individual’s data, it’s about restricting who can access AI-derived biological capability at all. This is what TwentyTwo was built for, before LatchBio acquired it in June 2026 to form Latch Biosecurity.

Both get called “AI bioprivacy.” Both are being shaped by AI in ways that are outrunning regulation. Worth looking at them side by side, because the implementation playbooks — and the regulatory gaps — are almost mirror images of each other.

Problem One: Genomic Data That Can’t Be Anonymized

Genomic data breaks the standard privacy toolkit in a specific way: you cannot irreversibly anonymize it. A hashed email address is genuinely useless without the key. A genome is not — it is inherently re-identifying, because it’s unique to you, shared in degraded form with every blood relative, and increasingly matchable against public genealogy databases even after names and dates are stripped out. Research on AI and genomic privacy notes that AI systems can reconstruct identity or infer sensitive attributes from “anonymized” genomic datasets through linkage and model-inversion attacks — the anonymization was never as durable as it looked.

That’s the problem Lifebit’s platform is built around, and their published “6-Step Guide to Genomic Data Privacy” is a reasonably complete snapshot of what an implementation actually looks like in 2026:

  1. Audit the data landscape — inventory every genomic data store, classify by sensitivity, score risk.
  2. Federate instead of centralize — “bring compute to data”: analysis executes at the site holding the data, not after the data has been copied out. This is also a direct answer to jurisdictional data-residency rules, since the data never crosses a border in the first place.
  3. Layer technical controls — AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.3 in transit, role-based access with MFA and time-limited tokens, differential privacy and k-anonymity on top of de-identification, and secure compute environments that block raw data downloads entirely.
  4. Govern access formally — a Data Access Committee, standardized request workflows, and consent tracked as a living record rather than a one-time checkbox.
  5. Automate compliance monitoring — an “airlock” that inspects every query result for re-identification risk before it’s released, plus real-time anomaly alerts and tamper-proof audit logs.
  6. Keep regulatory documentation current — compliance matrices mapped to HIPAA, GDPR, and FedRAMP, incident response playbooks, scheduled penetration testing.

The federated model deserves the emphasis it gets. Lifebit describes it elsewhere as a “peace treaty” between institutions that want to collaborate but are structurally unable to hand raw data to each other — hospitals bound by patient consent scope, biobanks bound by national data-residency law, pharma bound by IP concerns. Centralized-policy, decentralized-execution sidesteps all three: only summary statistics leave the firewall, and disclosure traps (like refusing to return results for cells with fewer than five individuals) stop small-group queries from becoming de-facto re-identification.

None of this is exotic. Differential privacy, secure enclaves, and federated learning are established techniques — a recent scoping review of privacy-enhancing technologies for biomedical AI rates federated learning as well-suited to regulatory alignment but vulnerable to gradient-reconstruction attacks without secure aggregation, and homomorphic encryption as strong but 10×–1000× slower than plaintext — fine for batch genomic analytics, unworkable for anything real-time. The honest summary: every privacy-enhancing technique buys privacy by spending either utility, latency, or infrastructure complexity. Nobody gets all three for free, and Lifebit’s stack is best read as a set of pragmatic trade-off choices, not a solved problem.

The Part Regulation Hasn’t Caught Up To

Here’s where it gets genuinely unresolved. GDPR and CCPA both center on a “right to be forgotten” — but that right assumes data lives somewhere as a record that can be located and deleted. Once genomic data has been used to train a model, it isn’t a record anymore — it’s embedded in the model’s parameters. Stanford Law’s analysis of this problem puts it plainly: deleting the original file doesn’t remove the learned pattern, and “it remains unclear how the right to be forgotten should apply to internal model parameters that encode learned patterns.”

Machine unlearning is the proposed technical fix, and it runs into a three-way tension: speed, privacy, and fairness pull against each other, because removing one person’s data point from a trained model can distort the statistics the model relies on for everyone else in that person’s demographic group — especially in a genomic context where population structure is the whole point. And genomic data is familial — it belongs to you and, in degraded form, to every blood relative you have. If one sibling consents to having their genome used and another demands deletion, individual-rights law has no clean answer, because the data point in question isn’t cleanly individual to begin with. This is the argument for moving toward collective or familial privacy rights rather than purely individual ones — a genuinely open regulatory question, not a solved one.

Problem Two: When “Bioprivacy” Means Restricting Capability, Not Protecting Data

TwentyTwo’s framing is almost the inverse. The risk isn’t that someone’s biological data leaks — it’s that AI has collapsed the expertise barrier that used to make engineering a dangerous pathogen a nation-state-scale undertaking. Per their Y Combinator profile, the founding premise is blunt: “AI is making biology easy to engineer. Life-saving drugs and therapies are accelerating, but so is the ability for bad actors to create a pandemic.” The acquisition announcement from LatchBio frames the company’s job as building systems that can “distinguish [the line between legitimate and malicious use] and apply safeguards or grant capabilities accordingly” — because that line is shifting from nation-states toward individuals as the tooling gets more accessible.

Concretely, this cashes out as synthetic nucleic acid order screening — the checkpoint where someone orders a custom DNA sequence from a synthesis provider. Screening has always had two layers: sequence screening (does this match a regulated pathogen database?) and legitimacy screening (does this customer have a real reason to order it?). The second layer has historically been the weak one, because it’s expensive: a 2026 Frontiers evaluation of AI-assisted legitimacy screening puts manual verification at roughly £73 per flagged order — too costly to apply broadly.

The same study benchmarked LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Grok 4, and others) on five verification tasks — institutional affiliation, institution type, email domain, sanctions-list screening, and searching for relevant prior work — using web search plus specialized tools like a sanctions-list API, Europe PMC, and ORCID. Gemini 2.5 Pro with tool access hit 89.8% accuracy against a 79.7% human baseline, at roughly $1.18 per customer including human review — about 10x cheaper than the ~$14 manual process. The paper names TwentyTwo and a peer, Aclid, explicitly as commercial actors building this category. TwentyTwo’s own materials describe the broader product as AI agents combined with traditional intelligence sources that assemble background checks “in minutes” with a complete audit trail for the human who makes the final call, plus biosurveillance work reportedly spanning 27 U.S. sites monitoring more than 13 million people and AI biosecurity evaluations that frontier AI labs have adopted.

The point isn’t the specific numbers — it’s the shape of the problem. Cheap, accurate AI screening is what makes universal legitimacy checks economically viable for the first time. That’s a genuine capability win. It’s also a new single point of failure: the screening model itself becomes the thing an adversary wants to fool, and there’s no established regulatory framework yet for auditing an AI system that’s making go/no-go decisions on which DNA sequences ship.

Where Regulation Actually Stands

Neither problem has settled regulatory footing, and they’re being pulled by different bodies of law.

On the data-privacy side, the EU AI Act classifies biometric categorization and identification as high-risk uses requiring risk management, data governance, and human oversight — but its Annex III high-risk obligations were pushed back to December 2, 2027 in a May 2026 agreement between Parliament and Council, so the binding compliance clock hasn’t actually started yet. GDPR still governs the underlying genomic data as a special category, but as covered above, it wasn’t written with model parameters in mind, and nobody has closed that gap.

On the biosecurity side, there’s essentially no equivalent statutory framework yet — synthetic nucleic acid screening is largely governed by voluntary industry standards and procurement requirements (e.g., US federal contracts increasingly requiring it) rather than binding law. That’s part of why commercial screening infrastructure like TwentyTwo/Aclid is filling the gap ahead of regulation rather than in response to it — the frontier AI labs adopting these evaluations are doing so voluntarily, not because a regulator requires it.

The throughline: in both cases, the technology (federated compute, differential privacy, LLM-based screening) is arguably ahead of the law that’s supposed to govern it. Lifebit’s implementation guide and TwentyTwo’s screening pipeline are both, in effect, private governance filling a gap that public regulation hasn’t caught up to — which is a reasonable stopgap, but not a substitute for the harder legal questions (familial consent, model unlearning, mandatory screening standards) that only legislatures and courts can actually resolve.

Sources

  • TwentyTwo — Biosecurity for Life Sciences
  • TwentyTwo | Y Combinator
  • LatchBio acquires TwentyTwo to form Latch Biosecurity
  • Evaluating AI-assisted customer verification for synthetic nucleic acid screening — Frontiers
  • Lifebit: How To Ensure Genomic Data Privacy — 6-Step Guide
  • Lifebit: Genomic Data Privacy — Enabling a Genomic Revolution
  • Lifebit: Why a Federated Analytics Platform is the Ultimate Data Peace Treaty
  • Artificial intelligence and genomic data privacy: Balancing innovation with security — NCBI
  • Safeguarding biomedical AI: privacy-enhancing technologies scoping review — PMC
  • Why AI Cannot Forget Genomic Data — Stanford Law School
  • EU AI Act, Annex III: High-Risk AI Systems
  • EU pushes AI Act deadlines for high-risk systems, including biometrics — Biometric Update

item.title: Annotating Cell Types: CellTypist, Marker Genes, and an LLM, Compared Honestly
item.dc:creator: Shubham Sendre
item.description:
What This Is (and Isn’t)

Once you’ve clustered a single-cell RNA-seq dataset, you’re left with the same question every time: what is cluster 4, actually? This post walks through three ways to answer that — a reference-based classifier (CellTypist), classical marker-gene scoring, and an LLM reading each cluster’s top differentially expressed genes — run on the same dataset, so their agreements and disagreements are directly comparable.

It is not a benchmark paper. One dataset, nine clusters, no ground-truth FACS labels to score against — just three legitimate methods, run side by side, with an honest look at where they line up and where the disagreement is actually informative rather than a bug.

The Dataset: PBMC3k

PBMC3k is 10x Genomics’ public demo dataset — 2,700 peripheral blood mononuclear cells, sequenced with an early 10x Chromium chemistry, and the same dataset the canonical Scanpy PBMC3k tutorial uses. It’s small, public, and has been independently annotated by enough people that its expected cell types (T cell subsets, B cells, monocytes, NK cells, dendritic cells, platelets) are well established — which makes it a reasonable dataset to sanity-check three annotation methods against, even without a formal ground truth.

Standard preprocessing: filter cells with fewer than 200 genes and genes in fewer than 3 cells, drop cells with more than 20% mitochondrial reads, normalize to 10,000 counts and log1p-transform, select the top 2,000 highly variable genes, PCA to 50 components, and Leiden clustering at resolution 1.0. This produced 2,698 cells across 9 clusters.

Method 1: Reference-Based Annotation with CellTypist

CellTypist is a logistic-regression classifier trained on large, curated reference atlases — here, the Immune_All_Low model, trained for fine-grained immune cell subtypes. It predicts a label per cell, plus a probability for every candidate label, and optionally runs majority voting: given an independent over-clustering (Leiden, in this case), it assigns the cluster’s dominant per-cell label to every cell in that cluster, smoothing out noisy individual calls.

Both outputs matter for different reasons: the per-cell labels reveal within-cluster heterogeneity a single cluster-level name would hide; the majority-voted labels give a clean, one-label-per-cluster summary that’s easier to report and compare against the other two methods.

Method 2: Marker-Gene Scoring — the Classical Baseline

No training, no reference atlas — just canonical PBMC marker gene sets (CD3D/CD3E for T cells, MS4A1/CD79A for B cells, GNLY/NKG7 for NK cells, CD14/LYZ for classical monocytes, FCGR3A/MS4A7 for non-classical monocytes, FCER1A/CST3 for dendritic cells, PPBP/PF4 for platelets, and CD8-specific markers for cytotoxic T cells). Each cluster’s mean sc.tl.score_genes score is computed against every marker set, and the cluster is assigned whichever set scores highest.

This is the annotation equivalent of a hand-tuned rule — transparent and fast, but only as good as the marker panel you wrote down in advance. It can’t discover a cell type you didn’t already have a gene list for.

Method 3: An LLM Reading Marker Genes

For each cluster, sc.tl.rank_genes_groups (Wilcoxon test) produces its top 10 differentially expressed genes. Those gene symbols — nothing else, no cluster statistics, no prior labels — are handed to an LLM with a fixed prompt asking for the single most likely PBMC cell type:

“Given the top differentially expressed marker genes for one cluster, return the single most likely immune cell type… Top marker genes (highest to lowest significance): {genes}”

Two choices matter for reproducibility here: the model is pinned to a specific version and called with temperature=0, so the same marker list produces the same label on every rerun rather than drifting between calls; and every prompt/response pair is logged and cached to disk, so re-running the offline script during iteration doesn’t re-call (or re-bill) the API for clusters that haven’t changed.

The appeal is obvious: zero marker-panel curation — the model brings its own prior knowledge of immunology instead of a hand-written gene list. The risk is just as real: an LLM can produce a fluent, confident, wrong label with no calibrated uncertainty attached, and it has no way to say “I don’t recognize this” the way a low CellTypist probability can.

Try It: Interactive Comparison

The panel below is a full marimo notebook running in your browser via WebAssembly (Pyodide) — no server, no Python install on your end.

One honest caveat on how this is built: none of scanpy, anndata, or CellTypist’s scikit-learn backend are verified to run inside a browser’s WASM sandbox, so all three methods above were run once, offline, and their outputs — UMAP coordinates, per-cell and per-cluster labels, confidence scores, the agreement statistics — were saved as small CSV/JSON files. What is genuinely live in the notebook: recoloring the UMAP by any of the four label sets, filtering cells by CellTypist confidence, and browsing the per-cluster table — all pure pandas/NumPy/Matplotlib, recomputed in your browser every time you touch a control.

Where the Methods Agree — and Where They Don’t

Cluster Cells Marker-gene baseline CellTypist (majority) Agreement
0 880 T cells Tcm/Naive helper T cells Broad match
1 314 T cells Tcm/Naive helper T cells Broad match
2 347 B cells B cells Exact match
3 491 Monocytes (CD14+) Classical monocytes Exact match
4 445 NK cells CD16+ NK cells Broad match
5 159 Monocytes (FCGR3A+) Non-classical monocytes Exact match
6 34 Dendritic cells DC Exact match
7 15 Platelets Megakaryocytes/platelets Exact match
8 13 CD8 T cells Tem/Trm cytotoxic T cells Broad match

At the broad cell-type level, the two methods agree on all nine clusters. Every disagreement is a resolution mismatch, not a contradiction: the marker-gene baseline’s fixed panel names a broad category (“T cells,” “NK cells”), while CellTypist’s finer reference model names a specific subtype within it (“Tcm/Naive helper T cells,” “CD16+ NK cells”). That’s the expected failure mode of a hand-picked marker panel — not wrong, just lower resolution than a model trained on a much larger labeled reference.

How much does CellTypist’s per-cell typing agree with the clusters themselves?

CellTypist assigns every cell a label independently — it never sees the Leiden partition. Comparing its raw per-cell labels against the Leiden clusters with the Adjusted Rand Index gives 0.449. That’s meaningfully below 1.0, and it should be: the confusion matrix in the notebook shows CellTypist splitting single Leiden clusters (especially cluster 0, the largest T-cell cluster) across several related subtypes — Tcm/Naive helper T cells, Tem/Effector helper T cells, Treg, MAIT cells — rather than just re-deriving the same 9 groups under a different name. A majority-voted, one-label-per-cluster summary (like the table above) is convenient, but it genuinely erases that heterogeneity.

Discussion: When to Trust Which

  • Broad-category calls are cheap to get right; subtype calls are where methods diverge. If you only need “lymphocyte vs. myeloid,” any of these three methods will likely agree. Subtype-level annotation is where the choice of method — and its reference panel’s resolution — actually matters.
  • CellTypist’s confidence scores are directly actionable. Because it outputs a real probability per cell, you can filter to “only the calls I’m confident in” and manually review the rest — see the confidence slider in the notebook above. Neither the marker-gene baseline nor a plain LLM label comes with a comparably calibrated uncertainty signal.
  • LLM annotation trades curation cost for hallucination risk. No marker panel to write and maintain, but also no guarantee the label is grounded in anything beyond the model’s prior — and unlike CellTypist, it can’t natively flag “this doesn’t look like any cell type I know.” Treat it as a fast first pass to be checked, not a final call.
  • None of this generalizes across tissue or disease state without re-checking. PBMC3k is about as friendly a dataset as scRNA-seq annotation gets — a well-studied tissue with a mature reference model. Solid tumor or disease-state datasets, where CellTypist’s training distribution is a worse match and marker panels are less standardized, will show more disagreement between all three methods than this post does.

Reproducing This

  • Offline stage (generate_artifacts.py): downloads PBMC3k, runs the standard Scanpy preprocessing/clustering pipeline, runs CellTypist (Immune_All_Low model with majority voting), scores the marker-gene baseline, calls an LLM per cluster for the third annotation, computes the agreement statistics, and writes the small artifacts this notebook loads. The LLM step reads its API key from the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable only — never hardcode it — and caches every response to disk so reruns don’t re-call the API for unchanged clusters.
  • Interactive stage (notebook.py): the marimo notebook above. Needs only numpy, pandas, matplotlib, and marimo — all WASM-compatible, which is why it can ship as a static page with no server behind it.
# offline (heavy env: scanpy, anndata, celltypist, anthropic)
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...
conda run -n scanpy python generate_artifacts.py

# interactive notebook, locally
conda run -n quarto-blog marimo edit notebook.py

# export the interactive layer to a static, browser-runnable bundle
conda run -n quarto-blog marimo export html-wasm notebook.py -o notebook_wasm --mode run

item.title: Segmenting Nuclei in H&E Images: A Morphometry Pipeline, Not a Diagnosis
item.dc:creator: Shubham Sendre
item.description:
What This Is (and Isn’t)

This post is about turning a microscopy image into a measurement table — segment the nuclei in an H&E-stained tissue patch, quantify them (count, area, shape), and score how good that segmentation actually is against expert ground truth.

It is not a diagnostic tool. I’m a bioinformatics engineer, not a pathologist. Everything here is engineering: given a segmentation, how do you honestly measure whether it’s any good, and how much does the choice of method actually matter?

The short answer, with numbers to back it up: a lot.

The Task: Instance Segmentation, Not Just “Find the Nuclei”

Nuclei in a dense tissue patch touch and overlap. The hard part isn’t distinguishing tissue from background — simple intensity thresholding gets you most of the way there. The hard part is separating individual nuclei that are touching, which is what turns this into an instance segmentation problem rather than a semantic one.

That distinction matters for evaluation too. A method can get the foreground region almost perfectly right while still merging a cluster of six nuclei into one blob — which is a serious error for any downstream measurement (cell counts, density, morphology), but invisible to a pixel-accuracy or plain Dice score. So this post scores both.

Two Methods, Scored Honestly

Classical: Otsu threshold → distance transform → watershed. Threshold the image, compute a distance-to-background map, find local maxima as seed points, and let watershed grow regions from those seeds. No training, no learned features — just intensity and geometry.

Deep learning: StarDist, using the pretrained 2D_versatile_he model (trained specifically on H&E-stained nuclei — no fine-tuning done here). StarDist predicts star-convex polygon shapes per nucleus directly, which handles touching nuclei far more gracefully than a purely intensity-driven watershed.

Evaluation: AJI and Panoptic Quality, not pixel accuracy. Aggregated Jaccard Index and Panoptic Quality are instance-aware — they penalize merged and split nuclei, not just boundary disagreement. I also report a plain foreground Dice score for reference, but it’s the weaker signal of the three.

Results on 4 MoNuSeg patches (256×256, held-out test split)

Method AJI Panoptic Quality Dice (foreground)
StarDist 0.655 0.642 0.820
Classical watershed 0.387 0.272 0.638

StarDist wins by a wide margin on every metric, and the gap is largest on Panoptic Quality — exactly the metric most sensitive to merge/split errors. Looking at the per-sample breakdown, the classical baseline’s failure mode is consistent: in dense clusters it over-segments, predicting far more instances than actually exist (92 predicted vs. 39 ground-truth nuclei in one patch) because intensity-based watershed markers proliferate wherever the distance transform has a local wobble. That’s the concrete cost of not learning shape priors.

None of this means classical watershed is useless — with a well-tuned marker distance it’s a legitimate, zero-training baseline for sparse, well-separated nuclei. It just doesn’t hold up on realistic tissue density.

Try It: Interactive Notebook

The comparison above isn’t fixed — you can change the classical baseline’s parameters and watch its score move in real time. The panel below is a full marimo notebook running in your browser via WebAssembly (Pyodide). No server, no Python installation on your end.

One honest caveat on how this is built: StarDist’s segmentation runs on TensorFlow, which cannot execute inside a browser’s WASM sandbox. So the StarDist masks you see below were computed once, offline, and are loaded here as precomputed arrays. The classical watershed baseline, the morphometric plots, and the AJI/PQ/Dice scoring, however, are all genuinely live — scikit-image and SciPy run natively in Pyodide, so moving the slider actually re-segments the image in your browser.

From Masks to Measurements

The point of segmentation, in most real workflows, isn’t the mask itself — it’s what you can measure from it. Once nuclei are labeled, regionprops turns each one into a row of a table: area, perimeter, eccentricity, solidity, centroid. That table is the actual deliverable — it’s what feeds downstream statistics, not the colorful mask image.

This is the throughline of the pipeline: image → instance mask → feature table → validated numbers, with the validation step (AJI/PQ against ground truth) treated as a first-class part of the pipeline rather than an afterthought.

Reproducing This

  • Offline stage (generate_artifacts.py): fetches 4 patches from the MoNuSeg dataset (CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0) via Hugging Face, runs StarDist inference, computes the classical baseline once, scores both against ground truth, and writes the small artifacts this notebook loads. Needs TensorFlow + StarDist — run it in its own environment.
  • Interactive stage (notebook.py): the marimo notebook above. Needs only numpy, pandas, matplotlib, scikit-image, scipy — all WASM-compatible, which is why it can ship as a static page.
# offline (heavy env)
conda run -n nuclei-seg python generate_artifacts.py

# interactive notebook, locally
conda run -n quarto-blog marimo edit notebook.py

# export the interactive layer to a static, browser-runnable bundle
conda run -n quarto-blog marimo export html-wasm notebook.py -o notebook_wasm --mode run

item.title: RO-Crate and Nextflow: Making Your Pipeline Outputs FAIR and Reproducible
item.dc:creator: Shubham Sendre
item.description:
The Problem RO-Crate Was Built to Solve

A folder of pipeline outputs is opaque. Raw files sitting on a server answer none of the questions anyone actually needs answered:

  • What tool produced this VCF? At what version?
  • What input data was used? Are the checksums the same?
  • Who ran this? When? On what infrastructure?
  • Can I re-run it and get the same result?

The bioinformatics community has tried to solve this before. Research Objects — the conceptual predecessor to RO-Crate — proposed bundling research materials with rich linked data metadata. The idea was sound. The adoption was not. The technology stack required (OWL ontologies, SPARQL, full RDF toolchains) was too steep for most working scientists and engineers.

RO-Crate is the pragmatic successor. It was designed, as Soiland-Reyes et al. put it, to use “just enough Linked Data” — structured metadata that is machine-readable and semantically interoperable, but accessible to anyone who can write JSON1.

What RO-Crate Actually Is

An RO-Crate is a directory — any directory — with a single file added: ro-crate-metadata.json. That file uses JSON-LD and schema.org vocabulary to describe what is in the directory, who created it, what software was involved, and how the contents relate to each other.

JSON-LD is the key design choice here. It looks like ordinary JSON, which means any developer can read and write it without learning a new toolchain. But it carries semantic meaning: every field maps to a well-defined concept in an internationally agreed vocabulary. A Person entity in your metadata means the same thing as a Person in a Harvard data repository or a European health data space.

The spec defines three types of entities:

Entity Type What It Describes Example
Root Data Entity The crate itself — the top-level research output The pipeline run directory
Data Entities Files and directories inside the crate results/annotated.vcf.gz, samplesheet.csv
Contextual Entities Things referenced from outside A Person, a SoftwareApplication, an Organisation

The FAIR Guiding Principles2 — Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable — are the stated goal. RO-Crate is the practical mechanism for achieving them without requiring semantic web expertise.

Two Levels of RO-Crate in a Nextflow Context

Before writing any JSON, it helps to understand that RO-Crate applies at two distinct levels in a Nextflow pipeline:

Level What It Describes When It Exists
Pipeline-level The workflow itself — purpose, authors, license, inputs, outputs Once per pipeline, committed to the repo
Run-level A specific execution — input files, parameters, container versions, timestamps Generated fresh per pipeline run

Both are valid RO-Crates. They serve different purposes. The pipeline-level one makes your workflow a citable, discoverable artifact on WorkflowHub. The run-level one is your audit trail and reproducibility record.

Pipeline-Level RO-Crate: Describing Your Workflow

The pipeline-level ro-crate-metadata.json lives in the root of your repository. It describes your workflow as a ComputationalWorkflow — a scientific artifact with a name, authors, license, and formal descriptions of its inputs and outputs.

The Minimal Structure

Every valid RO-Crate metadata file has two required entries in its @graph:

{
  "@context": "https://w3id.org/ro/crate/1.1/context",
  "@graph": [
    {
      "@id": "ro-crate-metadata.json",
      "@type": "CreativeWork",
      "conformsTo": {"@id": "https://w3id.org/ro/crate/1.1"},
      "about": {"@id": "./"}
    },
    {
      "@id": "./",
      "@type": ["Dataset", "ComputationalWorkflow"],
      "name": "my-annotation-pipeline",
      "description": "A Nextflow pipeline for variant annotation using VEP, FastQC, and MultiQC.",
      "license": "MIT",
      "version": "1.0.0",
      "programmingLanguage": {
        "@id": "https://w3id.org/workflowhub/workflow-ro-crate#nextflow"
      },
      "author": [{"@id": "#author-1"}],
      "input": [{"@id": "#input-samplesheet"}],
      "output": [{"@id": "#output-vcf"}]
    }
  ]
}

The first entry (ro-crate-metadata.json) is always the metadata descriptor — it points to ./ as its subject. The second entry (./) is the root dataset — your pipeline.

Adding Authors

{
  "@id": "#author-1",
  "@type": "Person",
  "name": "Shubham Sendre",
  "affiliation": "Invisibl Cloud Solutions Pvt. Ltd.",
  "url": "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000"
}

Use your ORCID as the @id if you have one — it makes the pipeline citable in academic contexts and is how WorkflowHub links pipeline authorship to your research identity.

Describing Inputs and Outputs

FormalParameter entries are what make the pipeline machine-readable. WorkflowHub parses these to display pipeline interfaces:

{
  "@id": "#input-samplesheet",
  "@type": "FormalParameter",
  "name": "input",
  "description": "Samplesheet CSV with sample IDs and paths to FASTQ files",
  "encodingFormat": "text/csv"
},
{
  "@id": "#output-vcf",
  "@type": "FormalParameter",
  "name": "annotated_vcf",
  "description": "VEP-annotated VCF with functional consequence predictions",
  "encodingFormat": "text/tab-separated-values"
}

Referencing Software Dependencies

Use bio.tools identifiers where they exist — they are the standard registry for bioinformatics tools and the identifiers WorkflowHub recognises:

{
  "@id": "https://bio.tools/vep",
  "@type": "SoftwareApplication",
  "name": "Ensembl VEP",
  "version": "110.1",
  "url": "https://www.ensembl.org/vep"
}

Add this to hasPart or softwareRequirements on the root Dataset node.

Run-Level RO-Crate: Provenance with nf-prov

The pipeline-level RO-Crate describes your workflow as a static artifact. Run-level provenance captures what actually happened in a specific execution.

This is where the W3C PROV data model3 becomes relevant. PROV defines a standard vocabulary for describing entities (data), activities (processes), and agents (people/software) and the relationships between them. The nf-prov plugin translates Nextflow execution events into a PROV-conformant RO-Crate automatically.

Enabling nf-prov

Add to your nextflow.config:

plugins {
  id 'nf-prov@1.2.2'
}

prov {
  enabled = true
  formats {
    rocrate {
      file = "${params.outdir}/pipeline_info/ro-crate-metadata.json"
    }
  }
}

What Gets Captured Per Run

After every pipeline execution, nf-prov writes an ro-crate-metadata.json into your output directory that records:

  • Workflow version (exact git commit or tag)
  • Input files with checksums (MD5/SHA256)
  • Output files with checksums and sizes
  • Start and end timestamps per process
  • Container image IDs used per process
  • Full resolved parameter set at runtime

A fragment of what the run record looks like:

{
  "@id": "#run-2026-04-15",
  "@type": "CreateAction",
  "instrument": {"@id": "main.nf"},
  "startTime": "2026-04-15T09:23:11Z",
  "endTime": "2026-04-15T11:47:32Z",
  "object": [{"@id": "inputs/samplesheet.csv"}],
  "result": [{"@id": "results/annotated.vcf.gz"}]
}

This is the difference between “I ran the pipeline” and “I can prove exactly what ran, on what input, at what time, and what came out.”

Publishing to WorkflowHub

WorkflowHub is the community registry for FAIR scientific workflows. It reads your pipeline-level ro-crate-metadata.json directly to:

  • Display pipeline metadata, authors, description, and inputs/outputs
  • Assign a DOI to your pipeline version, making it citable in publications
  • Link to bio.tools and Bioschemas entries for referenced software
  • Index your pipeline for discoverability across the research community

Registering is straightforward: provide a link to your repository or upload a zip, and WorkflowHub validates your RO-Crate and creates a landing page with a persistent identifier.

A DOI-backed WorkflowHub entry is a concrete portfolio artifact — a versioned, citable record with your name on it that you can link from a CV or LinkedIn profile.

Why This Matters Beyond Good Practice

Reproducibility is shifting from optional to expected. Journals and funders increasingly require that computational analyses be reproducible. An nf-prov RO-Crate is concrete evidence — not “here’s the code”, but “here’s the exact execution with checksums on every input and output.”

External delivery has a provenance question. Delivering pipeline outputs to pharma companies, hospitals, or research institutes often comes with the question: can you prove what ran? An RO-Crate run record is a ready-made answer that doesn’t require trust — it’s self-describing and verifiable.

Regulated environments are where this becomes load-bearing. Trusted Research Environments (TREs) — secure compute environments for sensitive clinical data used in NHS, UK Biobank, and EU health data spaces — require data provenance and audit trails by design. RO-Crate is one of the standards being evaluated and adopted to satisfy those requirements. That last point is where this gets genuinely interesting, and it’s where Part 2 of this series picks up.

Quick Reference: From Zero to FAIR Pipeline

Step Action Time
1 Create ro-crate-metadata.json in pipeline root 30 min
2 Add authors (with ORCID), description, keywords, I/O parameters 20 min
3 Add bio.tools IDs for your software dependencies 15 min
4 Enable nf-prov in nextflow.config 10 min
5 Run pipeline, inspect generated run-level RO-Crate 20 min
6 Register pipeline on WorkflowHub for a DOI 30 min

References

  1. Soiland-Reyes S et al. (2022). Packaging research artefacts with RO-Crate. Data Science. DOI: 10.3233/DS-210053
  2. Soiland-Reyes S et al. (2022). Creating lightweight FAIR Digital Objects with RO-Crate. Research Ideas and Outcomes, Vol. 8. DOI: 10.3897/rio.8.e93937
  3. Wilkinson MD et al. (2016). The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship. Scientific Data. DOI: 10.1038/sdata.2016.18
  4. Groth P, Moreau L (2013). PROV-Overview: An Overview of the PROV Family of Documents. W3C Working Group Note. https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-overview/
